The fee will impose disruptive checkout changes, new compliance and technology burdens, risk loss of customers to competitors just outside the city limits, and create strained, conflict‑prone register interactions that small and medium retailers are ill‑equipped to absorb.

Briefing (prepared on behalf of the Local Retailers Coalition for Councilmember Garcia and policy aide): we unequivocally oppose the proposed 10¢ single‑use plastic bag fee as drafted because it will impose disruptive checkout changes, new compliance and technology costs, greater register conflict, and the real risk of customer loss to competitors just outside city limits—harms that fall disproportionately on small and medium retailers with thin margins and limited staff capacity.  

Evidence basis and uncertainty: our assessment follows the city staff memo and the Riverton addendum and aligns with municipal evaluations showing operational burdens and variable environmental outcomes (see Convery et al., evaluation of Ireland’s levy; Welsh Government carrier‑bag charge evaluation, 2016; and the reports summarized in the staff materials); however, precise estimates of customer migration, net revenue effects, and long‑term net environmental benefits require local, longitudinal data and thus involve extrapolation beyond current Riverton/municipal findings.  

Impacts on customers: staff and external analyses note regressive effects are possible — low‑income shoppers make more frequent small purchases and are more sensitive to per‑transaction fees — and the draft’s current narrow exemptions do not adequately address that risk.  

Requested, evidence‑grounded remedies to materially reduce retailer burdens (please indicate which you will pursue before the committee work session): (a) lower the fee to 2–3¢ or phase in over 12–18 months (reduces per‑transaction impact and gives time for POS/IT adaptation); (b) exempt small retailers (by revenue or floor area) and expand low‑income transaction exemptions (avoids disproportionate compliance costs and regressivity); (c) allow retailers to retain a capped portion of collections or provide direct reimbursement for POS upgrades (offsets compliance/technology costs); or (d) pause for a one‑year pilot/local impact study before citywide rollout (prevents premature disruption while collecting local evidence).

Appendix — prepared on behalf of the Local Retailers Coalition: four key claims, each with what staff/Riverton/regional studies actually show and where our interpretation extends beyond that evidence.  

Retailer operational burdens — Evidence: the city staff memo flags increased transaction time, POS/configuration and compliance needs; the Riverton addendum reports only modest reporting changes and few formal complaints to date (see staff memo; Riverton addendum); Coalition interpretation: we expect materially larger disruption for small/medium retailers (training, lost throughput, POS upgrade costs, increased labor) than Riverton’s early experience indicates, which is an extrapolation from broader municipal reports to our local retail mix.  

Cross‑border customer loss — Evidence: staff memo notes cross‑border migration as a theoretical risk but presents no local data; Riverton’s early data show no measurable migration so far; regional comparisons show such effects can occur in certain geographies (see regional comparison summary). Coalition interpretation: we project meaningful customer loss risk over time in border neighborhoods, especially among price‑sensitive shoppers — a reasonable concern but one that goes beyond existing local evidence and depends on local store density and proximity to lower‑fee jurisdictions.  

Low‑income/regressivity — Evidence: staff materials and peer evaluations document that per‑transaction bag fees can be regressive because lower‑income households make more frequent small purchases and are more price‑sensitive; Riverton’s limited exemptions have not fully addressed this per the staff FAQ. Coalition interpretation: absent stronger, broader low‑income exemptions our members’ low‑income customers will be disproportionately affected in practice; that is an application of general findings to our local retail footprint rather than a directly measured local outcome.  

Environmental outcomes — Evidence: the staff memo and published evaluations (e.g., Convery et al. 2007 on Ireland; Welsh Government evaluation 2016) show large reductions in counted single‑use bags in some jurisdictions, while other analyses (e.g., CalRecycle 2018 and select municipal reports) document substitution to thicker plastic or paper bags and variable net environmental benefits; Riverton’s early data are limited. Coalition interpretation: we therefore urge caution that a 10¢ fee may deliver smaller net environmental gains than claimed and could produce unintended substitution effects; this is a policy judgment informed by mixed evidence rather than definitive proof.
